title: Rafael and the Harbor
premise: In the port city of Vessamare, Lior Thornbury, a pearl diver's daughter indentured to the Harrow & Vale Trading Company, keeps her head down and her ledger clean — until the seasonal closing of the harbor bridge strands her inside the company compound with a dying clerk, a stolen manifest, and proof that the company has been drowning divers in debt they can never repay. As winter tides seal the harbor, Lior must decide whether to burn the evidence to protect the found family she's built among the dockworkers or risk everything to get it aboard the morning ship and into the hands of a colonial magistrate. She chooses the record over the escape, testifying at cost of her indenture, and ends the book freed but unmoored — walking out across the reopened bridge with nothing carried but the truth and the people who stayed.
about_author: Beatrix Sandoval is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing shipping ledgers from colonial trading posts. Her fiction is known for its salt-stained realism and its insistence that ordinary clerks and divers, not captains, are where history actually happens.

chapters.title: What the Tide Takes
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. We meet her measuring her life in portable things: her mother's diving knife, three coins, a debt ledger she can recite by heart. The chapter establishes her indenture to Harrow & Vale and her quiet habit of memorizing numbers no one asks her to remember. Emotional beat: wary competence masking grief for her drowned father.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The last cart crosses the harbor bridge before the season's storms; Lior misses it by an hour because Clerk Aldous Fen ordered her to re-copy a manifest. Trapped inside the compound with dockworkers, divers, and company men, she feels the walls tighten. Emotional beat: claustrophobia and the first flicker of resentment toward the company that owns her years.

chapters.title: A Ledger of Drowned Men
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, with a scene from dockworker Maren's perspective. Lior discovers entries showing divers billed for equipment lost with their bodies — debts inherited by their children. Fen catches her reading and, instead of reporting her, coughs blood into his handkerchief and says, 'Someone should know.' Emotional beat: horror transmuting into purpose.

chapters.title: Found Family, Borrowed Time
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The dockworkers' winter community comes alive: shared stew, smuggled songs, Maren teaching Lior that loyalty can be chosen. But company overseer Brannick begins counting heads and searching bunks, hunting a missing page Fen tore from the manifest. Emotional beat: warmth sharpened by encroaching fear; Lior lets herself belong.

chapters.title: Fen's Confession
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Dying, Fen dictates the full scheme to Lior — falsified weights, bribed magistrates, the morning ship that carries the 'clean' books out each spring. He gives her the torn page and begs her to get it on the record before the victors' historians write their version. Emotional beat: a deathbed passing of the torch, terror and resolve entwined.

chapters.title: Brannick's Offer
chapters.summary: Brannick's POV. Suspecting Lior, Brannick offers her freedom papers if she surrenders the page and names her allies. He is not a cartoon villain — he genuinely believes order requires sacrifice, and he once was indentured too. Lior stalls. Emotional beat: temptation rendered human; duty and survival pulling in opposite directions.

chapters.title: The Search
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Brannick ransacks the workers' quarters; Maren hides the page inside a child's doll and takes a beating rather than give up Lior. The found family closes ranks without being asked. Lior realizes her testimony will cost them all if she fails. Emotional beat: fierce solidarity, guilt, and the price of survival made literal.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. On the frozen seawall, Lior and Maren admit what they are to each other, knowing the morning tide forces a choice: Maren can smuggle Lior onto a fishing skiff to safety, or Lior can board the company ship carrying the false books and testify to the magistrate aboard. Emotional beat: tender, aching clarity — love expressed as letting the other choose.

chapters.title: The Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Climax. Lior boards the ship under pretense of delivering Fen's effects, evades Brannick through the hold, and places the true ledger and her sworn statement before Magistrate Oyelaran as the lines are cast off. Brannick confronts her on deck; the magistrate reads. Emotional beat: white-knuckle suspense resolving into the terrifying calm of having spoken.

chapters.title: Across the Bridge
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, coda in spring. The inquiry vindicates the divers; Brannick faces his own reckoning; Lior's indenture is voided. She walks the reopened bridge with Maren, carrying only what can be carried — which now includes a future. Emotional beat: quiet, earned hope; the truth survived the crossing, and so did she.
